subject: economics
title: Sustainable Growth Stretch
welcome_lead: Growth at any cost, or growth that lasts? Weigh up benefits, environmental damage and inequality in this exam-style stretch.
meta_desc: GCSE Economics exam-style adventure on growth: sustainable growth, costs/benefits and policy evaluation.
final_note: Growth examined from every angle. Inflation up next!

concepts.def: Growth without depleting environment for future.
Uneven distribution of income or wealth.
Side-effects of production on third parties.
Max output economy can sustain long-term.
Growth that benefits all income groups.

walkthroughs.body_html: Higher wages and consumption, more tax revenue (better schools/NHS), lower unemployment, more business confidence. UK growth since 1950 has lifted living standards dramatically — but unevenly.
Environmental damage (pollution, CO₂), resource depletion, inequality (top 10% gain more), stress and overwork. Top-band answers always mention these alongside benefits.

Green tech, renewables, carbon pricing and circular economy aim to deliver growth without wrecking the climate. Trade-off: green policies may cost jobs short term but build long-term productive capacity.

mcqs.q: Which is a COST of rapid economic growth?
options: Higher tax revenue
Environmental pollution
Lower unemployment
More consumer choice
Maximum short-term GDP
Growth that doesn't deplete the environment for future generations
Growth above 10% per year
Growth only in services

mcqs.q: How is economic growth shown on a Production Possibility Curve?
options: Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
By an outward shift of the entire curve — reflecting an increase in productive capacity through more or better resources, technology, or skills.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Growth is shown by moving from inside the curve to a point on the curve.

mcqs.q: What causes the supply curve to shift?
options: Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Changes in production costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of producers, expectations — anything affecting supply other than the good's own price.
When demand rises, the supply curve shifts right to meet it.
Fixed costs are paid once and variable costs are paid daily.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
options: Fixed costs never change at all, ever.
Fixed costs are paid once and variable costs are paid daily.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Fixed costs don't change with output (e.g. rent, salaries); variable costs change directly with output (e.g. raw materials, hourly wages).
